newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Broker rates Belgian retailer Quick buy.
newsitem.headline: Broker rates Belgian retailer Quick buy.

text.p: Shares in Belgian hamburger chain Quick jumped 3.50 percent on the Brussels bourse on Wednesday as Antwerp-based broker Bank Deelen rated the stock a buy.
"People have been focusing on the negatives such as the impact of mad c0ow disease, but I looked at it and found some positive points," analyst Geert De Mesure said by telephone.

He said first half 1997 restaurant sales had been the same as in the corresponding six months of last year, and the second half would be better than 1996 -- the period in which Quick suffered most from the mad cow disease fallout.
Quick shares opened at 2,000 francs but rose steadily to 2,070 as people latched onto the buy recommendation.
De Mesure said his price target was between 2,400 and 2,520 francs based on a fair valuation of 20 times projected 1997 earnings or 18 times 1998 earnings.
He noted that the company's tax rate would fall in 1997 to 27 percent from an average of 38 percent in 1994 and 1995.
Because of what he termed a "disastrous" 1996, the tax rate then was only 17.5 percent.
Quick had also increased the number of franchised restaurants and taken advantage of a sale and rent-back offer.
The chain, which had 371 restaurants at the end of last year when sales were 21.5 billion francs, would open 30 more this year, De Mesure said in his research note.
He said the decline in new restaurants from 45 in 1996 was a result of the company management's determination to limit the debt/equity ratio to 80 percent -- a level it slightly exceeded in 1996.
While the increase in franchising had a negative impact on operating margins, it also had a positive effect on the return on capital employed, he said.
The Bank Deelen analyst said that earnings per share, which dropped last year to 58 francs from 112 in 1995, would rise to 120 francs this year and 140 francs in 1998.
He estimated dividend per share of 32 francs this year and 35 francs in 1998 against 30 in 1995 and 1996.
The firm had taken steps to improve profitability, with cost of basic goods set to fall six percent and administrative costs stabilised in absolute terms.
This, coupled with rising turnover as a result of improving sales and new restaurant openings, augured well for the firm.
"1996 was a bad year. But there is nothing to prevent Quick regaining its growth stock status," De Mesure said.
